::: {#exr-prac-binom-lik}
#### Binomial likelihood (adapted from @dobson4e, Chapter 3)

Let $Y \sim \text{Binomial}(n, \pi)$,
so that

$$
\p(Y = y \mid \pi) = \binom{n}{y} \pi^y (1-\pi)^{n-y},
\quad y \in \{0, 1, \ldots, n\}.
$$

Assume $0 < y < n$ so the MLE lies in the interior of $(0, 1)$.

**(a)** Write the log-likelihood $\ell(\pi; y)$ for a single observation $y$.

**(b)** Derive the score function $\ell'(\pi; y) \eqdef \deriv{\pi}\ell(\pi; y)$.

**(c)** Set the score equal to zero and solve for $\hat\pi_{ML}$.
Confirm that $\hat\pi_{ML} = y/n$.

**(d)** Compute the second derivative $\ell''(\pi; y)$ and verify that it is negative,
confirming a maximum.
:::

:::{#sol-prac-binom-lik}

**(a)**

$$
\ba
\ell(\pi; y)
&= \logf{\binom{n}{y} \pi^y (1-\pi)^{n-y}}
&& \text{(log of the binomial PMF)}
\\
&= \logf{\binom{n}{y}} + \logf{\pi^y} + \logf{(1-\pi)^{n-y}}
&& \text{(log of a product)}
\\
&= \logf{\binom{n}{y}} + y\logf{\pi} + (n-y)\logf{1-\pi}
&& \text{(log of a power)}
\ea
$$

The first term does not depend on $\pi$,
so it drops out of every derivative with respect to $\pi$.

**(b)**

$$
\ba
\ell'(\pi; y)
&= \deriv{\pi}\sb{\logf{\binom{n}{y}} + y\logf{\pi} + (n-y)\logf{1-\pi}}
&& \text{(log-likelihood from (a))}
\\
&= \deriv{\pi}\logf{\binom{n}{y}} + \deriv{\pi}\sb{y\logf{\pi}} + \deriv{\pi}\sb{(n-y)\logf{1-\pi}}
&& \text{(linearity of differentiation)}
\\
&= 0 + \deriv{\pi}\sb{y\logf{\pi}} + \deriv{\pi}\sb{(n-y)\logf{1-\pi}}
&& \text{(derivative of a constant)}
\\
&= \deriv{\pi}\sb{y\logf{\pi}} + \deriv{\pi}\sb{(n-y)\logf{1-\pi}}
&& \text{(drop the zero term)}
\\
&= y\deriv{\pi}\logf{\pi} + (n-y)\deriv{\pi}\logf{1-\pi}
&& \text{(constant multiple rule)}
\\
&= y\frac{1}{\pi} + (n-y)\deriv{\pi}\logf{1-\pi}
&& \text{(derivative of $\log$)}
\\
&= y\frac{1}{\pi} + (n-y)\frac{1}{1-\pi}\deriv{\pi}(1-\pi)
&& \text{(chain rule)}
\ea
$$

The inner derivative is:

$$
\ba
\deriv{\pi}(1-\pi)
&= \deriv{\pi} 1 - \deriv{\pi} \pi
&& \text{(linearity of differentiation)}
\\
&= 0 - \deriv{\pi} \pi
&& \text{(derivative of a constant)}
\\
&= 0 - 1
&& \text{(derivative of $\pi$ with respect to itself)}
\\
&= -1
&& \text{(subtract)}
\ea
$$

Substituting the inner derivative back in:

$$
\ba
\ell'(\pi; y)
&= y\frac{1}{\pi} + (n-y)\frac{1}{1-\pi}(-1)
&& \text{(inner derivative is $-1$)}
\\
&= y\frac{1}{\pi} - (n-y)\frac{1}{1-\pi}
&& \text{(multiply by $-1$)}
\\
&= \frac{y}{\pi} - \frac{n-y}{1-\pi}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= \frac{y(1-\pi)}{\pi(1-\pi)} - \frac{(n-y)\pi}{\pi(1-\pi)}
&& \text{(write both terms over the common denominator)}
\\
&= \frac{y(1-\pi) - (n-y)\pi}{\pi(1-\pi)}
&& \text{(combine the fractions)}
\\
&= \frac{y - y\pi - n\pi + y\pi}{\pi(1-\pi)}
&& \text{(expand the numerator)}
\\
&= \frac{y - n\pi}{\pi(1-\pi)}
&& \text{(cancel $y\pi$)}
\ea
$$

**(c)**

Setting $\ell'(\pi; y) = 0$:

$$
\ba
0 &= \frac{y - n\pi}{\pi(1-\pi)}
&& \text{(score from (b))}
\\
0 &= y - n\pi
&& \text{(multiply both sides by $\pi(1-\pi)$)}
\\
y &= n\pi
&& \text{(add $n\pi$ to both sides)}
\\
\hat\pi_{ML} &= \frac{y}{n}
&& \text{(divide both sides by $n$)}
\ea
$$

**(d)**

$$
\ba
\ell''(\pi; y)
&= \deriv{\pi}\sb{\frac{y}{\pi} - \frac{n-y}{1-\pi}}
&& \text{(score from (b))}
\\
&= \deriv{\pi}\sb{y\pi^{-1} - (n-y)(1-\pi)^{-1}}
&& \text{(write the fractions as negative powers)}
\\
&= \deriv{\pi}\sb{y\pi^{-1}} - \deriv{\pi}\sb{(n-y)(1-\pi)^{-1}}
&& \text{(linearity of differentiation)}
\\
&= y\deriv{\pi}\pi^{-1} - (n-y)\deriv{\pi}(1-\pi)^{-1}
&& \text{(constant multiple rule)}
\\
&= y\paren{-\pi^{-2}} - (n-y)\deriv{\pi}(1-\pi)^{-1}
&& \text{(power rule)}
\\
&= y\paren{-\pi^{-2}} - (n-y)\paren{-(1-\pi)^{-2}}\deriv{\pi}(1-\pi)
&& \text{(chain rule, outer function $u^{-1}$)}
\\
&= y\paren{-\pi^{-2}} - (n-y)\paren{-(1-\pi)^{-2}}(-1)
&& \text{(inner derivative from (b) is $-1$)}
\\
&= -y\pi^{-2} - (n-y)(1-\pi)^{-2}
&& \text{(multiply)}
\\
&= -\frac{y}{\pi^2} - \frac{n-y}{(1-\pi)^2}
&& \text{(write the negative powers as fractions)}
\ea
$$

Since $y \geq 0$, $n - y \geq 0$, and $y$ and $n - y$ are not both zero,
$\ell''(\pi; y) < 0$ for every $\pi \in (0,1)$.
So $\ell$ is strictly concave,
and its critical point $\hat\pi_{ML} = y/n$ is its global maximum.

:::
